textbookText: 18.4 Spectrum of Light The band of seven colors obtained, when a white light splits into its constituent colors on striking the surface of a glass prism is called a spectrum." In other words, a spectrum is a collection of dispersed light that gives wavelength composition. When white light is incident on a prism, it is splitted into different constituent colours which are deviated through different angles. Such dispersed light, when received on the screen or photographic plate, forms a spectrum. There are two types of spectrum; pure spectrum and impure spectrum. Pure Spectrum When the white light is dispersed through a glass prism, and split colours do not overlap to each other (all colors can be seen distinctly) on the screen as shown in figure 18.2, then the corresponding spectrum is pure spectrum of light. A better method of obtaining a pure spectrum is to use a parallel beam of light as in an instrument called a spectrometer. For this an illuminated slit is placed at the principal focus of a converging lens so that a parallel beam of light emerges from it, and falls on a prism. Refraction through the prism splits up the light into Physics, Grade 11 | 366

separate parallel beams of different colours, each of which is brought to its own focus in the focal plane of a second lens. The resulted pure spectrum may be formed on a white screen, or can be viewed through a magnifying eyepiece. Therefore, for obtaining pure spectrum following conditions should be satisfied.

1. Slit should be narrow. 2. Rays coming out from convex lens should have parallel incidence. 3. Prism should be in condition of minimum deviation. 4. Emerging light rays should be focused by achromatic lens.
[Fig.18.5, Pure spectrum]

Impure Spectrum When the white light is dispersed through a glass prism and the spiltt colours overlap on the screen so that all colours cannot be seen distinctly as in figure 18.6, then the corresponding spectrum is called an impure spectrum of light.

18.5 Angular Dispersion
[Fig.18.7, Angular dispersion produced by a prism] Physics, Grade 11 | 367

Angular dispersion is defined as the difference in the angles of deviation of two extreme colours (violet and red) of the spectrum of white light. That is Angular dispersion, a = v – r . . . (1) Consider a beam of white light passing through a glass prism so that different colours are deviated by different angles. Deviation of yellow colour is nearly average of deviation of all other colours. Therefore, yellow colour is taken as mean colour, and mean deviation of light is measured by the deviation of yellow light. The angle of deviation produced by violet light is more than that produced by red light as shown in figure 18.7. That means r<y<v and a = A(v – r). This expression gives the angular dispersion of light through a glass prism.
18.6 Dispersive Power
Awhite light passing through a prism suffers both deviation and dispersion. The dispersive
power of the material of prism is its ability to disperse the constituent colours of incident light,
and it is measured in terms of the ratio of angular dispersion between two extreme colours to
the deviation produced by mean colour. Dispersive power has no unit and dimension. It is
denoted by  and given by
ω = δv − δr δ
or, ω = (μv − μr ) (μ −1)
This is an expression for dispersive power of the material of a prism.

18.7 Aberration of Light in Lenses The deviation in the shape, size and position of the actual image from the image predicted by lens formula is called aberration. It is defined as a property of optical systems such as lenses that causes light to be spread out over some region of space rat her than being focused to a point. An optical system with aberration will produce a blurred image that is not sharp, and cannot be seen with clarity. There are different types of aberration; Chromatic aberration, Spherical aberration, etc. a. Chromatic Aberration A lens may be considered as the combination of prisms so it exhibits prismatic behavior. If rays of light parallel with the principal axis incident on the surface of the lens then they split up into different constituent colours after refraction. "An inability of a lens to focus all colours of light at a single point on the principal axis is called chromatic aberration. It is also known as axial or longitudinal aberration. The chromatic aberration is measured in terms of the difference in focal lengths of red colour (fr) and violet colour (fv).
